slides.0.title: Introducing South African wine
slides.0.subtitle: History and modern revival
slides.1.title: The Cape colony and the first wine
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Jan van Riebeeck was commissioned to build a fort and farming community at the Cape as a supply station for ships
slides.1.highlights.1.title: 1655 and 1659
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The first Cape vineyard was planted in 1655; on 2 February 1659 the first wine was made from Cape grapes (French Muscadel)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Constantia
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Governor Simon van der Stel acquired the roughly 750-hectare Constantia estate in 1685; sources differ slightly on dates of his appointment and purchase
slides.1.content: Keep the storyline: a Dutch East India Company supply station → the first wine → Constantia becomes a famous estate.
slides.2.title: Settlers, fame and disaster
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The Huguenots
slides.2.highlights.0.content: From 1688 French Huguenot refugees arrived at the Cape, bringing viticultural and winemaking experience; their descendants still shape the industry
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The fame of Constantia
slides.2.highlights.1.content: In 1816 André Jullien ranked Constantia wines in the top category of his world classification; Napoleon is said to have asked for them in exile on St Helena
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Phylloxera
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Phylloxera reached the Cape in 1866 and caused devastation that took more than 20 years to recover from
slides.2.content: Constantia's sweet wines were once world-famous, but nineteenth-century disasters and market shifts set the industry back.
slides.3.title: The KWV era and the modern revival
slides.3.highlights.0.title: KWV in 1918
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The government funded the formation of KWV in 1918; it later set policy and prices for the whole industry, restricted yields and imposed distillation quotas, and by 1924 about 95% of vineyard owners were members
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Boycotts and opening up
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Boycotts through the twentieth century held back exports; after apartheid ended in the late 1980s and 1990s the industry returned to international markets
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Towards consumer wine
slides.3.highlights.2.content: In 1990 under 30% of the harvest became consumer wine; by 2003 it was over 70%
slides.3.content: The key turning point of modern South Africa is the opening up of the 1990s and the shift from distilling stock to quality wine.
